title: China rehearses landing troops over a floating bridge of civilian ships opposite Taiwan
dek: Satellite images show a weeks-long amphibious drill in Fujian's Dacheng Bay, on the eve of Taiwan's local elections. Beijing calls its training 'entirely legitimate and reasonable'.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China's military has spent most of November rehearsing a way of landing troops and equipment by lashing civilian vessels together into a makeshift floating bridge, in a bay on the coast facing Taiwan, according to satellite imagery reviewed by analysts and reports. The drill in Dacheng Bay, in Fujian province about 280 km from Taiwan's main island, was still under way on Friday, a regional security official said, according to reports.

Taiwan's defence ministry said it was aware of the activity, including the use of civilian vessels, and was assessing what it meant for security in the Taiwan Strait and for regional peace. Asked about recent drills, China's defence ministry said on Thursday that its training was "entirely legitimate and reasonable", according to reports. Taiwan holds local elections on Saturday.

## What the images show

The exercise was first spotted on 1 November, according to a report by the geospatial firm ingeniSPACE. Images taken between 1 and 16 November show vessels repeatedly forming and taking apart a floating bridge about 800 metres long. Eight civilian vessels took part: four barges, two semi-submersible ships and two powered vessels, supported by four landing craft, smaller boats and Chinese navy ships nearby. Imagery from the commercial satellite operators Vantor and Planet Labs showed the same activity, reports said.

No purpose-built military bridging equipment was seen, which ingeniSPACE said pointed to improvised landing infrastructure. Its chief operating officer, Jason Wang, said the People's Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing "low-signature methods" of supplying an invasion force, and that bridging heavy equipment ashore from deeper water could give an attacker more possible landing points along Taiwan's coast. He said radar jamming had also been observed in the area.

The security official said the drill was designed to "practise the swift seizure of small islands" along the first island chain, and was part of this year's "All-Military Strategic Exercise", routine but later in the year than usual. The official cautioned against overstating its value, saying barges would be "live targets" in a war, according to reports.

## Background

Taiwan disclosed amphibious drills in Dacheng Bay in September 2023 and September 2024, both using roll-on, roll-off ferries. The bay lies near Dongshan Island, which Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited in 2024. China regards self-governed Taiwan as its territory and has never renounced the use of force to bring it under its control; Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's claim. Military attachés in Asia say China keeps refining coastal drills because an amphibious crossing of the strait would be one of the hardest military operations to attempt.

## Why it matters for India

The Taiwan Strait is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, and Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced computer chips, which go into the phones, cars and electronics that India imports and assembles. Any blockade or conflict there would disrupt supply chains that Indian manufacturers, including the electronics assemblers the government is courting with production incentives, depend on. India has no formal diplomatic relations with Taipei but has expanded trade and technology ties with Taiwan. India's foreign ministry has not commented on the drill.

## What happens next

Taiwan's local elections on Saturday will be watched for any Chinese military activity around the island. Taiwan's defence ministry publishes daily counts of Chinese aircraft and ships near Taiwan; analysts will also be watching whether the Dacheng Bay exercise ends or moves to a new stage.
